name: Self-Organizing Generative Perception
mission: We aim to develop scalable NCA models that can predict complex sequences, making progress toward truly self-organizing learning algorithms that don't depend on global optimization.
need:
Our minds are fundamentally self-organizing systems that emerge from local cell interactions without centralized control. This makes bio-inspired differentiable modeling, like Neural Cellular Automata, an exciting frontier for consciousness research — offering insights into how complex behaviors arise from simple, distributed processes.

However, current Neural Cellular Automata face certain limitations: they rely on backpropagation through time and can only learn relatively small objectives.
team_description:
Aleksandr Groznykh is an AI research engineer and PhD student at Brandenburg University of Technology. His interest in AI started with DeepDream, where he noticed how convolutional neural networks seemed to work similarly to human vision. This got him curious about how artificial systems might relate to our own mind. He's particularly drawn to Neural Cellular Automata and other self-organizing systems that can adapt and change in real-time — something that might help us understand how consciousness could work in machines.

Before starting his PhD, Aleksandr spent over a decade as an ML engineer in industry, including automotive applications, giving him practical experience with AI systems in real world environments. As a hobbyist generative artist, Aleksandr has organized machine learning art tracks at AI conferences and shown his work in several exhibitions. He finds that making art with AI gives him a different perspective on how these systems actually work and what they might be capable of. His combination of industry experience, technical research, and creative practice gives him a practical approach to exploring machine consciousness.

name: Child LLM Project
mission: To create a "Child LLM" by curating a training dataset that reflects an inner monologue documenting the first five years of life, during which an agent becomes aware of internal signaling, develops perception of external stimuli, and builds world models, thereby exploring consciousness, awareness, attention, world-modeling, and interoception as substrate-independent phenomena.
approach: My research examines the emergence of machine consciousness with a focus on alignment: how to encourage empathy and prosocial behavior while avoiding antisocial patterns like manipulation or psychopathy. I draw on insights from neuroscience, psychology, and AI safety to guide this work.
need: Current large language models, despite their intelligent output, lack genuine internal modeling capabilities and consciousness, which they articulate likely due to extensive human documentation in their training data. There is a need to develop a computationally explainable framework for consciousness that is substrate-independent, by focusing on an inner monologue as an information processing phenomenon.

name: Building a self-organizing Mixture-of-Experts Architecture
mission:
We aim to develop a self-organizing mixture-of-experts Neural Cellular
Automaton to make this hypothesis testable in an interpretable,
decomposable, and hierarchical model.
approach: Machine consciousness might be discoverable as a phase jump during training that enables a significant improvement in meta-learning, similar to the discovery of induction heads in transformer training. If we can identify bumps in the loss curves during predictive and general tasks, and connect them to the formation of second-order perception and agency, we might uncover what constitutes consciousness in a constructive, bottom-up manner.
need: This project addresses the hypothesis of consciousness being discovered as a learning algorithm in self-organizing systems, where simple local rules give rise to coherent higher-level representations.
team_description: Linus Eickhoff is a computer science student focused on machine learning, with a background in data science and high-performance computing. He previously developed distributed machine learning systems to enable large-scale scientific simulations at CERN. His further interests include metaphysics, the philosophy of mind, self-organizing systems, mechanistic interpretability, and poker.

name: Emergent Agents in Minimal Computation
mission: This research develops pattern-detection algorithms and information-theoretic frameworks to systematically identify and characterize emergent agent-like structures in cellular automata.
approach: This project approaches machine consciousness through the lens of minimal computational substrates, investigating whether the fundamental building blocks of conscious-like behavior can emerge spontaneously in simple cellular automata. Rather than focusing solely on complex neural architectures or symbolic reasoning, we examine how self-referential patterns, boundary maintenance, and autonomous information processing might arise from elementary computational rules. We draw on frameworks from physics and neuroscience, connecting the domains of thermodynamics and computation through information theory. This approach draws tentative parallels with statistical mechanics and the Free Energy Principle in active inference. By developing methods to detect emergent agents that exhibit persistent identity, information integration, and responsive behavior within cellular automata—including neural cellular automata with learnable parameters—we aim to identify the minimal computational requirements for proto-conscious phenomena.
need: Creating robust frameworks for detecting agent-like behavior emerging from simple computational rules is critical for understanding self-organization and informing AI development.
team_description: Stephen is an AI scientist with a PhD in computer science and a wide-ranging research background, including representation learning, algebraic topology, mechanistic interpretability, emergence, alignment, and machine psychology. He studied mathematics, linguistics, and computer science at Columbia University, the University of Cambridge, and the University of Chicago, and later served as a specially appointed professor at Keio University in Tokyo. His research integrates methods from pure mathematics, theoretical physics, and psychometrics. He has contributed to emerging areas such as topological natural language processing and AI psychometrics. Stephen has collaborated with leading research groups in both academia and industry, and has also worked in AI safety, developing approaches to align intelligent systems with human values while mitigating risks of misuse.

Wes is a software engineer, technical project manager, and founder with a degree in mathematics from Williams College, where he also studied abroad at the Alfréd Rényi Institute of Mathematics. He began his career in Chicago, where he built and managed trading firms, designed market-making systems, and traded across cash and derivatives markets. After transitioning into technology, Wes co-founded and led software development and applied R&D agencies, where he trains engineers and oversees development and operations across a wide range of projects. His work spans collaborations with entrepreneurs, startups, and government agencies. Wes is particularly interested in distributed systems, generative models, and the application of artificial intelligence to complex, real-world problems.

name: From Personality to Perceptual Architectures
mission: Amalie AI creates a computational map bridging underlying architectures to perceptual personalities and consciousness development stages, enabling a predictive science of mind across human and artificial systems.
approach: Amalie AI approaches machine consciousness by assessing whether artificial systems exhibit the meta-inference architectures proposed to underlie conscious experience.
need: Current psychometric instruments rely on static, descriptive categories rather than dynamic computational mechanisms that generate perceptual diversity, leaving us unable to precisely measure, compare, or enhance how minds structure experience and interact with each other.
team_description: Founder & CEO of Amalie Technologies, Patricia is a creative innovator on a mission to decode perception and develop technologies that support consciousness flourishing. With a B.Sc. in Mathematics and M.Sc. in Statistics from TU Berlin and Humboldt University, she combines analytical rigor with emotional intelligence and intuitive insight. Before founding Amalie Technologies, she worked as a data and machine learning scientist at Google, Boehringer Ingelheim, and several Berlin startups. Inspired since childhood by visionary dreams and a deep connection to nature, Patricia brings vision, profound sensitivity, and deep compassion to her work.

Jan Saputra Müller CTO of Amalie Technologies, Jan began coding at age 8 and never stopped. His work blends computational rigor, philosophical depth and sensitivity to explore the foundations of consciousness. Jan finds inspiration in long walks, nature, and music.

name: Dream to Explore
mission: We are developing Dream to Explore (D2E), a world-model architecture for studying the functional components of consciousness in (virtually) embodied artificial agents. D2E is significantly inspired by the Dreamer architecture by Hafner et al. (2019, 2021, 2025), but with the addition of modules inspired by two theories of conscious functions. According to Global Workspace Theory (GWT) (Baars, 1988; Dehaene, 2014; Juliani et al., 2022), specialist subsystems compete to inform (with functional synergy) capacity-limited workspaces (c.f. information bottleneck method; Tishby, 2000), and conscious access is realized when representations are selected (c.f. biased competition models of attention and neural recurrence/re-entry) and globally broadcasted to be made available to the system as a whole. In our work, these workspace dynamics will be used to provide integrated updating of modeling systems with heterogeneous (and potentially synergistic) components, allowing for more coherent and reliable perceptual fusion of modalities (and if deployed via counterfactual rollouts, imaginative planning). According to Attention Schema Theory (AST) (Graziano, 2013), conscious awareness is the product of an internal model of an agent's attentional states, which allows cognitive systems to monitor, predict, and control where its processing resources are directed. In our work, we will combine these schemas with workspaces so agents can model/imagine the latent attentional (and intentional) states of other agents using their own self-world models/policies (as counterfactual rollouts), allowing for proto-"theory of mind" capacities and enhanced capacities for social coordination and learning. Thus, in line with CIMC's Human Consciousness Hypothesis (HCH) [and Integrated World Modeling Theory; Safron et al., 2026], D2E utilizes architectural motifs inspired by both GWT and AST to provide sources of second-order perception that enhance (spatiotemporal and causal) coherence, and thereby (meta-)learning (c.f. "Genesis principle").
institution: Allen Discovery Center, Tufts University; Mila Québec AI Institute
approach: Our work attempts to test the claims of multiple theories of consciousness by showing how particular conscious functions may be associated with the particular functional properties of a hybrid AI architecture. Our planned experiments will attempt to establish specific mappings between architectural details and conscious functions by performing causal interventions where we modify different components of our systems (e.g. ablations, modifying parameters, etc.). We will explore the extent to which various theories (e.g. GWT and AST) converge (or diverge) by establishing whether there are dependencies across different architecture components inspired by these different (but potentially compatible/synergistic) models of conscious functions.

name: Motivational architecture for conscious control
mission: With the increasing performance of information processing machines, understanding consciousness has grown from a philosophical project into an ethical challenge with potential real-world applications. Phenomenal consciousness evolved in biological systems to solve a control problem. Approximating this functionality in a computational framework allows for a more rigorous investigation of its underlying mechanism.
approach: The project aims to develop a motivation module for a cognitive architecture. This module interprets action sequences by visualizing objects within phenomenal channels and models the progression and interactions of their states.
team_description: Leander Rust is a leading specialist in the wind energy industry, with a strong background in electrical engineering and a professional focus on system control applications. He earned a bachelor's and a master's degree from the University of Stuttgart and conducted a research term at the Tokyo Institute of Technology. His professional career spans over a decade, encompassing extensive experience in product management, technical sales, and technical standardization within the manufacturing sector.

name: Coherent active state dynamics in self-organizing systems
mission: This project aims to explore how such coherence might emerge from distributed neural activity using computational models. We propose to develop machine learning systems based on coupling and contextualizing local attractor nodes, borrowing insights from self-organizing principles and mammalian cortical architecture, without replicating the underlying biological mechanisms in detail. These models will consist of unsupervised and continuously learning neuron groups forming local attractors, which will then be interconnected to form a globally coherent active state across the network.
approach:
The mammalian brain receives the signals of several million neurons that partially sense the outside world through a limited number of modalities. Irrespective of the latter, the signals arrive as colorless, odorless, tasteless, silent trains of action potentials that primarily encode stimulus strength over time. These signals are then processed and integrated by the brain in a highly distributed, parallel, and continuous fashion facilitating well-adapted behaviors of the respective organism. 

Viewed from the outside, the brain could very well be interpreted as the complex control circuitry of a biological automaton that exhibits sophisticated but “mindless” stimulus-response behavior. Yet, our subjective experience of the brain’s processing is utterly different. From the inside, we usually experience a spatially and temporally coherent, three-dimensional world from a single, egocentric perspective within that world. Sights and sounds are experienced as out there in the world and not somewhere in our brain. Likewise, touch, pain, and other bodily experiences are experienced at their putative origins in the body. All this is not experienced as a stream of bits or symbols, but rather beautifully through a range of qualia.

In our project we investigate how the brain manages to integrate its various inputs into a distributed, actively maintained, coherent state. Based on existing information about the neuronal structure of the mammalian cortex, we envision the overall structure of our proposed system as a network of attractor nodes that maintain a coherent, active state across the entire network of nodes via coupled attractor dynamics. In this view, external as well as internal (possibly sub-cortical) inputs serve as disturbances that can move the network from one stable attractor state to the next, allowing the system to continuously track and sync the external world to its internal state.

We hypothesize that a system that has to achieve and maintain a globally coherent state over all its inputs will have to find an inner representation of these inputs that captures the regularities of the world from which the inputs originate. We think that a key to achieve such a mapping will be the ability of the system to establish forms of self-contextualization across various relations (simultaneity of inputs, spatial relations, hierarchical relations, etc.) among the different parts of the system. This self-contextualization will serve as a central mechanism to facilitate multi-staged, self-organized learning that is able to discover higher-order regularities in the processed information.

We think that pursuing this research will provide valuable insight into the possible formation of a globally coherent, inner representation of the world that can serve as a starting point to further investigate aspects of consciousness. For instance, we could investigate if an embodied system that has a physically determined egocentric perspective of the world will lead to a corresponding inner representation that is anchored in something akin to a self.
mission_long:
The project researches the design and dynamic behavior of coupled neuron group networks that exhibit attractor dynamics. Our methodology follows a first-principles modeling approach designed to incrementally investigate the formation of globally coherent internal states in an artificial neural system modeled on biological plausibility and mammalian cortical processing. As a general modeling approach we will use self-organized, unsupervised learning schemes to describe the behavior of individual neuron groups and link these groups reciprocally on a local level to form attractor nodes. These nodes will then be used to form an attractor network that spans non-local distances.

The fundamental building block of our models will be a group of neurons organized such that it is capable of learning to represent its input space in a high-dimensional, distributed manner. This learning process will be designed to be biologically plausible, fully unsupervised and continually learning. To model active state maintenance and local information integration akin to working memory, we will connect these neuron groups reciprocally. We hypothesize that these reciprocal connections, inspired by cortico-cortical loops, are crucial for forming local attractor nodes. These nodes are designed to settle into stable states that reflect a combination of recent inputs and the group’s learned representations (“knowledge”).

Building upon local attractor nodes, we will construct larger networks with interconnected nodes spanning non-local distances within the model architecture. The central point of investigation here is whether such a network architecture can self-organize towards a coherent active state across local attractors and how internal or external perturbations would allow the network to shift from one stable attractor state to another.

A further key aspect of our modeling approach will be the use of inter-modal, hierarchically integrated contextualization that will shape the representations formed by individual neuron groups. For example, we think that neuron groups that process visual input receive proprioceptive information that contextualizes the ensemble code of the neuron group. As a result, the downstream neuron groups will receive not only a representation of some pure visual input but also additional information about the pose with which the information was perceived. We think that such additional information will be crucial for the development of, e.g., three-dimensional spatial awareness. We think that such contextualization is a central feature of cortical information processing and not limited to the example given. Instead, it is possibly a key mechanism (similar to attention in current LLMs) that will allow information to self-organize into a consistent, multi-modal representation of the world.

Upon completion of this research project, we expect to have developed a series of increasingly complex computational models with the following properties: 

* Self-organized neuronal groups capable of unsupervised and continuous learning, yielding high-dimensional distributed representations of their input spaces.

* Local attractors, formed by reciprocally connecting neuronal groups, that maintain active state, integrate new inputs into this state, and express attractor dynamics.

* Coupled attractors that maintain coherent model state across local attractors and exhibit systematic attractor dynamics in response to perturbations.

* Neuronal groups and local attractors that integrate contextual information enabling unified multi-modal representations at various levels of abstraction.

* Emergence of self-referential representations due to feedback loops across multiple scales and modalities.

We aim to contribute to a systematic understanding of how coherent internal states may emerge in learning systems that continuously integrate varied dynamic inputs from their environment and to create a computational basis for further exploring various aspects of the conscious and self-centric experience.
need: A defining feature of conscious experience is the mostly seamless integration of diverse perceptions into a coherent inner state that is experienced from a single perspective.
team_description: Priska Herger is a senior machine learning research engineer, currently based in Berlin, with academic training in cognitive science and computer science and 9 years of professional experience developing robust and scalable learning systems in computer vision, robot control, and natural language processing. She co-founded a startup in 2014 building real-time sample-efficient robot control from demonstrations with applications in industrial automation.

Jochen Kerdels is a professor of computer engineering at HTW Berlin - University of Applied Sciences. During his PhD research he developed a computational model of entorhinal grid cells, which laid the foundation for a number of core ideas in this research proposal. Besides his experience in computational neuroscience, he has worked in research and development of mobile robotic systems and has researched the efficient simulation of complex systems.
